sources.title: Why languages disappear
sources.body: Linguists estimate that around seven thousand languages are spoken today, but a large proportion of them may no longer be spoken by the end of this century. Languages rarely disappear suddenly. Instead, speakers gradually shift to a more dominant language that offers better access to education, jobs and media. Parents may stop passing their first language on to children, believing it will hold them back. When a language is lost, communities can lose traditional knowledge that is embedded in its vocabulary, such as names for local plants and their uses. Recording elderly speakers helps to preserve this knowledge, but documentation is not the same as revival, which depends on people choosing to use the language every day.

sources.title: Farming under solar panels
sources.body: Solar farms need large areas of land, which can bring them into competition with agriculture. Agrivoltaics offers a possible solution by combining the two on the same site. Solar panels are mounted high enough above the ground for crops to grow or animals to graze beneath them. In hot, dry regions, the partial shade from panels can reduce water loss from soil and protect some crops from heat stress, sometimes improving yields. Sheep can graze under panels and keep grass short, reducing maintenance costs. Not every crop benefits, however, since many need full sunlight. The approach also requires higher and more expensive mounting structures, so its success depends on careful design and the local climate.

sources.title: Front-of-pack food labels
sources.body: Nutrition information on the back of food packaging is often detailed but difficult to interpret quickly. To help shoppers make healthier choices, several countries have introduced simpler labels on the front of packages. Australia and New Zealand, for example, use a voluntary system that rates foods with stars, while other countries use colour-coded warnings for high levels of sugar, salt or fat. Studies suggest that clear labels can shift purchases towards healthier products and encourage manufacturers to improve recipes. However, voluntary schemes may be used mainly on products that score well, which limits their usefulness. Some researchers therefore argue that front-of-pack labels should be made mandatory.

sources.title: Tsunami warning systems
sources.body: A tsunami is a series of powerful waves usually caused by an undersea earthquake. In the open ocean, tsunami waves may be less than a metre high, but they travel extremely fast and grow much taller as they approach the coast. Warning systems use seismic stations to detect large earthquakes and ocean sensors that measure changes in sea level. When a threat is confirmed, alerts are sent to authorities and the public. Warnings are less useful for communities very close to the earthquake, where waves may arrive within minutes. For this reason, people in coastal areas of New Zealand are taught that a long or strong earthquake is itself a natural warning, and that they should move to higher ground immediately without waiting for an official alert.

sources.title: Crowdfunding scientific research
sources.body: Scientific research has traditionally been funded by governments, universities and large foundations. In recent years, some researchers have turned to crowdfunding, asking members of the public to contribute small amounts online. Crowdfunding can support projects that struggle to win traditional grants, such as early-stage ideas or research on topics that attract public interest, like local wildlife. It also encourages scientists to explain their work in accessible language, which can increase public engagement with science. However, the amounts raised are usually small, and projects with appealing stories may succeed more easily than those that are important but less exciting. Crowdfunding is therefore best seen as a supplement to conventional funding.

sources.title: Congestion charging
sources.body: Congestion charging requires drivers to pay a fee to enter busy parts of a city at certain times. The aim is to reduce traffic by encouraging some people to travel at different times, use public transport or combine trips. Cities such as London and Stockholm have introduced such schemes, and traffic in the charged zones fell noticeably after the charges began. The revenue can be invested in public transport, which makes alternatives to driving more attractive. Opponents argue that the charges are unfair to people who must drive for work and may harm businesses in the zone. In Stockholm, public opinion was initially hostile, but support grew after residents experienced the reduction in congestion.

sources.title: Antarctic krill
sources.body: Antarctic krill are small, shrimp-like animals, but they are one of the most important species in the Southern Ocean. They feed on tiny algae, including algae that grow under sea ice, and are themselves eaten by whales, seals, penguins and fish. Because so many predators depend on them, changes in krill populations can affect the whole ecosystem. Scientists are concerned that shrinking sea ice may reduce the food available to young krill in winter. Krill are also harvested commercially, mainly for fish farm feed and dietary supplements. The fishery is managed by an international commission that sets catch limits, but some conservation groups argue that fishing should be kept away from areas where predators feed.

sources.title: Exercise and mental health
sources.body: The physical benefits of exercise are well known, but a growing body of research shows that exercise also supports mental health. Regular physical activity has been linked to lower rates of depression and anxiety, and in some studies, exercise programmes have reduced symptoms of mild to moderate depression about as effectively as other common treatments. Scientists believe several mechanisms are involved, including changes in brain chemistry, better sleep and a sense of achievement. Exercise does not need to be intense to help; regular walking can be beneficial. Group activities may offer additional benefits through social contact. Nevertheless, experts caution that exercise should complement, rather than replace, professional treatment for serious mental illness.

sources.title: Printed books and e-books
sources.body: When e-books first became popular, many commentators predicted that printed books would soon disappear. That has not happened. In many countries, sales of e-books grew quickly and then levelled off, while printed books have remained popular. E-books are convenient, especially for travellers, and allow readers to adjust text size. Printed books, however, offer a physical experience that many readers value, and they do not require a device or battery. Some research suggests that readers remember the layout of printed pages, which may help them locate information later. Rather than replacing print, e-books appear to have become one option among several ways of reading.

sources.title: The water footprint of food
sources.body: The water footprint of a food measures the total amount of fresh water used to produce it, including rain that falls on crops and water used for irrigation and processing. Animal products generally have larger water footprints than plant foods, because animals must be fed crops over many months. However, water footprints need to be interpreted carefully. Water used in a rainy region where it is plentiful has very different consequences from irrigation water taken from rivers in a dry region. For this reason, some researchers focus on water scarcity rather than total volume. Consumers who want to reduce their impact can benefit from understanding where and how their food is produced, not just which category it belongs to.

sources.title: Wildlife corridors
sources.body: When natural habitats are divided by roads, farms and towns, animal populations can become isolated in small patches. Isolated populations are more vulnerable to disease, inbreeding and local disasters such as fire. Wildlife corridors are strips of habitat that link these patches, allowing animals to move, find mates and recolonise areas where populations have disappeared. Corridors can be as simple as a line of native trees along a stream, or as large as bridges built over highways. In Australia, rope bridges have helped tree-dwelling animals such as possums cross roads safely. Designing effective corridors requires knowledge of how particular species behave, since a corridor that suits birds may be useless for small mammals.

sources.title: How encryption protects data
sources.body: Every time someone shops online or sends a private message, encryption helps keep the information secure. Encryption converts readable data into a scrambled form that can only be read with the correct key. Modern internet security relies heavily on public-key cryptography, in which each user has two keys. A public key, which can be shared freely, is used to lock a message, while a private key, kept secret, is needed to unlock it. The security of these systems depends on mathematical problems that are extremely difficult for current computers to solve. Researchers are concerned that powerful quantum computers could one day break some of these systems, so new encryption methods are already being developed.

sources.title: The Great Artesian Basin
sources.body: The Great Artesian Basin lies beneath about a fifth of Australia and is one of the largest underground water resources in the world. Rain that falls on its eastern edge slowly seeps into layers of sandstone and moves through the rock over thousands of years. Because the water is under pressure, it can rise to the surface through bores without pumping. For more than a century, this water has allowed pastoral farming and towns to exist in dry inland regions. However, many early bores were left to flow freely into open drains, wasting large amounts of water and reducing pressure. Government programmes have since capped many bores and replaced open drains with pipes, helping pressure to recover in some areas.

sources.title: Teenagers and school start times
sources.body: During adolescence, the body clock shifts so that teenagers naturally feel sleepy later at night and find it harder to wake early. Early school start times can therefore leave many students chronically short of sleep. Lack of sleep has been linked to poorer concentration, lower grades and a higher risk of accidents among young drivers. Some schools that have delayed their start times by around an hour have reported improvements in attendance and alertness. Changing schedules is not simple, however. Later starts can affect bus timetables, after-school sports and parents' work arrangements. Supporters argue that these practical obstacles should be weighed against the clear evidence about adolescent sleep.

sources.title: Bees in the city
sources.body: Beekeeping has become a popular hobby in many cities, with hives appearing on rooftops, balconies and community gardens. Urban environments can offer bees a surprising variety of flowers in parks and gardens, and some city hives produce more honey than rural ones. However, researchers have raised concerns. In some cities, the number of managed honeybee hives has grown so rapidly that there may not be enough flowers to feed them all. Honeybees may then compete with wild bees, which are often more threatened. Experts suggest that people who want to help pollinators may achieve more by planting a diversity of flowering plants than by installing new hives.
